lessons.title: SDLC Overview
lessons.concept: The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a structured process for planning, creating, testing, deploying, and maintaining software. It provides phases and activities that help teams deliver quality software systematically.
lessons.formula: Common phases: Requirements -> Design -> Implementation -> Testing -> Deployment -> Maintenance.
lessons.worked_example: For a banking app: gather requirements (features/security), design architecture/UI, implement code, test functionality/security, deploy to users, and maintain with updates/fixes.
mistakes: Thinking SDLC ends at deployment (maintenance is ongoing)
Skipping requirements/design and jumping directly to coding
Assuming one rigid process fits all projects
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Common SDLC Models
lessons.concept: Different SDLC models organize phases differently. Waterfall is linear and sequential; iterative/incremental builds in cycles; Agile emphasizes adaptive planning, short iterations, and continuous feedback. Model choice depends on project needs, uncertainty, and stakeholder involvement.
lessons.formula: Waterfall: sequential phases. Agile: iterative sprints/increments with feedback. Iterative: repeated refinement cycles.
lessons.worked_example: A project with stable, well-defined requirements may suit a more sequential approach, while evolving product requirements may benefit from iterative/Agile delivery.
mistakes: Believing Agile means no planning or documentation
Assuming Waterfall allows easy late changes without cost
Treating model names as strict without understanding their practices
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Quality, Testing, and Maintenance
lessons.concept: Quality activities span the SDLC, including reviews, testing, and change management. Testing verifies behavior against requirements at different levels. Maintenance addresses bug fixes, enhancements, and adaptation to changing environments after release.
lessons.formula: Maintenance types (common): corrective (fix bugs), adaptive (environment changes), perfective (improvements), preventive (reduce future issues).
lessons.worked_example: After release, a security patch is corrective/preventive maintenance, while adding a new feature requested by users is perfective/enhancement work.
mistakes: Treating testing as a single end-phase activity only
